When choosing a career, the most important aspect would be to ...

subQuestions.questionText: An important strategy to maintain an effective study plan could include ONE of the following:

An effective study plan must stay flexible: adjusting activities when needed keeps you on track, whereas rigidly following every planned activity does not allow for progress checks.

options.B: Organise all the required assessment tasks

Among its statutory functions, the CCMA assists in establishing workplace forums; it does not organise financial support, promotions or discipline.

options.B: organise legal and financial support for workers.

options.D: inspire sincerity and discipline among workers.

subQuestions.questionText: Assessing an environmental project means to ...

Correct answer: D — consider the effect of recycling waste on your community. (1)

To assess a project is to evaluate its effects/impact; the other options are actions you would take, not an assessment.

options.A: reduce your carbon footprint in order to prevent air pollution.
options.B: minimise the use of electricity and water in your household.
options.C: propose ways to source grey water when and where possible.
options.D: consider the effect of recycling waste on your community.

subQuestions.questionText: The following are examples of fitness exercises to strengthen your core muscles:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — Crunches, sit-ups and push-ups. (1)

Crunches, sit-ups and push-ups all target the core (abdominal and trunk) muscles; sprints, lunges, skipping and squats are mainly lower-body or cardio exercises.

subQuestions.questionText:

An evidence-based research method used by the media to expose public matters concealed by people in power.

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer in full sentences.

Differentiate between the responsibilities of national and provincial governments in ensuring safe and healthy living conditions for all citizens.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response that contrasts the two levels. Any ONE of:
• National government creates/amends/implements/approves laws that promote safe and healthy living for the whole country, whereas provincial government creates and implements laws that affect its own province only.
• National government establishes legislation and standards for the safe and healthy living of the nation, whereas provincial government ensures local governments conform with these national policies.
• National government coordinates and monitors national programmes on safe and healthy living, whereas provincial government implements the policies in line with these programmes.
• National government provides support and funding and regulates the provision of health and safety services in the country, whereas provincial government provides financial, human and technical resources to local government to deliver the services.
• National government intervenes where provinces lack capacity to implement health and safety programmes, whereas provincial government ensures the national interventions are carried out.
• National government conducts budgetary processes and allocates to provinces based on need, whereas provincial government further allocates budgets to local municipalities according to their needs.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain ONE way in which you could adapt community sports/games to accommodate people with different disabilities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Pair people with disabilities with able-bodied people and rotate teams, so the able-bodied act as a support base in completing the activity.
• Adjust the activity by using equipment that accommodates disabled people, so the activity is fair to all and ensures safety.
• Use pictures to explain or modify the rules instead of only doing it verbally, to accommodate people who may have a disability.
• Adjust times and allow for breaks between activities, so disabled people can recover from exhaustion.
• Adapt the size of the playing ground or infrastructure to allow flexibility and be user-friendly where people use equipment to support their disabilities.
• Introduce disability-friendly games that are inclusive of everyone.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss ONE benefit of visualising the information that you study.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. It may help you to:
• Make sense of what you are studying and store it in long-term memory, making it easier to recall.
• Pay full attention and be more focused on what you are studying, making it easier to understand and memorise.
• Capture and retain a large amount of information, as the picture in your mind is a summary of the overall content.
• Pair information and concepts with meaningful images, strengthening the way you learn and increasing the chance of remembering.
• Process visual information more efficiently than text, as graphic presentations enhance understanding.
• Stimulate your imagination through photographs, charts and diagrams, enabling you to process information faster.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.passageText:
THE POWER OF OUR BELIEF SYSTEM

'Our belief system, unlike ideologies, is an invisible force behind our behaviour.'

[Adapted from The Power of our Belief System by Krysta Martynes]
subQuestions.questionText:
Read the source above and answer the question. Write your answers in full sentences.

State TWO factors which may have shaped your belief system.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each of TWO responses. Any TWO of:
• Early relationships with family and/or friends.
• Significant experiences you may have had in life.
• Positive or negative events/situations you have been exposed to.
• Influential people/influencers, e.g. people you regarded as role models.
• The religion you have followed since the early stages of your life.
• Cultural/traditional beliefs, faith and customs of the community, and values learnt from the family/environment you grew up in.
• The type of media you have been exposed to.
• The way you were brought up, educated or taught.
(2 x 1) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term ideologies.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Ideologies are any ONE of:
• Ideas that define a particular group of people, which may be political, social or economic ideas.
• The principles inherent to a group of people that describe what they believe in.
• Ideas that a group of people adhere to and that form part of their distinct identity.
• Mindsets that a society conforms to and that form the operating principles for that society.
• Thoughts or philosophies ascribed to a group of people that define their uniqueness.
• Beliefs that influence a group of people and shape how they think about the world.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest ONE way in which your belief system could influence your personal lifestyle choices. Motivate your answer. (No marks are awarded for examples.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Your beliefs about the type of lifestyle you want in future may affect the goals you set and the career choices you make.
• The morals and values you believe in may influence the friends you choose, the activities you engage in, the clothes you wear and how you embrace your identity.
• The lifestyle you choose to follow may be influenced by false beliefs you developed from life experiences.
• What you believe to be right about your physical and emotional well-being could determine whether you make decisions that benefit or harm your overall health.
• Wrongly believing that nothing works out for you may cause you to lose faith in things that could work, leading to decisions that hamper your personal and professional growth.
• How much you value the environment could affect how you conduct yourself in your surroundings, as you would be mindful of acceptable and unacceptable behaviour.
(1 x 2) (2)

questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 2: Basic Conditions of Employment Act — a worker's umbrella
questions.passageText:
BASIC CONDITIONS OF THE EMPLOYMENT ACT — A WORKER'S UMBRELLA

South African labour laws are amongst the best in the world today, as the Constitution has established labour law rights very strongly, and over time trade unions have also been able to provide further input into labour laws.

At the centre of labour legislation is the Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA), 1997 (Act 75 of 1997). Neither the employer nor the worker can ignore the conditions outlined in the BCEA, especially with regard to the regulations of a job contract as stipulated in the Act.

Every employer is legally obliged to provide all workers with a contract no later than the first day of employment. Employers are therefore well advised to enter into a job contract with a worker. It is also a fact that very few workers actually read the job contract before signing it.

Even though South African labour laws are fairly progressive, child labour, for instance, continues to exist in a variety of labour sectors in the country. Therefore, it is important that employers have a good understanding of the BCEA to ensure that they operate in a manner that is fully compliant with labour laws.

[Adapted from http://www.chamlabour.co.za. Accessed on 2 May 2022.]

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term job contract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. It may refer to:
• A written agreement between the employer and the worker that offers clear guidelines and expectations of the job.
• A binding document between employer and worker that specifies the worker's duties, responsibilities and obligations.
• A signed agreement between the employer and the worker that is bound by law.
• Legal written guidelines that aim to promote a good working relationship between employer and worker.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO ways in which trade unions could assist workers in addressing non-compliance with working conditions.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each of TWO responses. Trade unions could:
• Conduct regular surveys with members on non-compliance.
• Run induction workshops on labour matters and educate members on how to identify poor labour practices.
• Provide methods for workers to report non-compliance, without fear of victimisation.
• Organise legal strikes/protests/mass action/picketing or submit petitions dealing with non-compliance.
• Enforce labour laws on behalf of members.
• Monitor whether new policies or procedures disadvantage workers, acting as an impartial party.
• Empower workers to monitor and take ownership of their own working conditions.
• Update workers through forums on workplace practices affecting them.
• Advise workers on how to complete reports on non-compliance.
• Investigate claims, negotiate on behalf of workers and represent them in meetings, disciplinary hearings or labour disputes.
(2 x 1) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA), 1997 (Act 75 of 1997) protects under-aged children from working in a formal work environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• The responsibilities of a formal job may add stress to a child's life, as they may not be emotionally ready to deal with the challenges and failures of tasks.
• A formal environment may expose under-aged children to inappropriate situations, unlawful activities or dangerous environments and people they cannot cope with, endangering their health and safety.
• Early engagement with the demands of the adult world may leave children unable to deal with their childhood ending too soon.
• Under-aged children may be unskilled for specific jobs, making them too labour-intensive for their physical capacity.
• Children working at such a young age may be deprived of their legal and democratic right to education.
• Children earning money at a vulnerable stage may spend it unwisely or be financially exploited by adults.
• Young working children may be abused, exploited or underpaid and may unknowingly become victims of human trafficking or slavery.
• Young children may adopt bad habits from adults, endangering their health, mental well-being and safety.
• The Act regards 'a child as not a legal person', so a child is protected from legal processes that may occur in a formal work environment.
• Children have little information about their rights and may easily be abused, made to work long hours and not paid appropriately.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

subQuestions.questionText: How could an employer assist a young worker to minimise the consequences of misreading or not reading a job contract?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. Employers could:
• Ensure the lawyers drawing up the contracts simplify the language, so workers who are not fluent readers can understand what they read and sign.
• Allow workers to read contracts at home or provide electronic copies, so they do not feel pressurised and can read in their own time.
• Have translators or interpreters available and explain the contract to first and second additional language speakers, since the language may be difficult for such workers.
• Set aside a specific date and time, or conduct inductions, where workers are assisted by an HR practitioner, trade union members or pro-bono legal advisers to clarify queries, preventing misunderstanding and helping workers make informed decisions.
• Include animations, drawings or simulations in the contract, so workers with disabilities or learning difficulties clearly understand their conditions of service.
• Ensure contracts are legible and neatly typed, so workers do not misunderstand the content.
• Ensure the agreed conditions are not written in fine print, so workers do not overlook important details.
• Allow employees to ask questions about the contents, ensuring the content is interpreted correctly.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

subQuestions.questionText: Assess TWO advantages for an employer who provides workers with a job contract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. A job contract may:
• Minimise incidents of non-compliance the employer has to deal with daily and send a clear message about the employer's legal rights in the event of a breach or labour dispute.
• Help the employer establish the necessary structure and order in the workplace, reducing possible risks and penalties.
• Protect the business through policies included in the contract, reducing the possibility of legal claims against the employer.
• Protect sensitive company information through confidentiality clauses in the contract.
• Ensure the employer provides a full written job description, giving a reference if workers do not fulfil their duties.
• Safeguard the employer by preventing workers from becoming competitors after leaving, by forbidding them to sell the same products or services.
• Be used to attract highly skilled, sought-after workers, ensuring good candidates do not consider working for the competition.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

subQuestions.questionText: Examine why it is important for a worker to review a job contract. In EACH answer, also indicate how reviewing it may benefit the worker.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award THREE marks each for TWO well-explained responses (reason + how it works + benefit to the worker). Any TWO of:
• You may realise your job description has changed or you have gained new skills and are not being compensated accordingly, enabling you to renegotiate your salary.
• Your working conditions may need to improve to comply with applicable labour law, and ensuring amendments are made means you are legally entitled to more conducive conditions.
• The company may upgrade equipment to meet new technological advances, and as a worker you may need upskilling, so you can hold the employer accountable for the relevant training.
• The employer may amend the contract to accommodate reasonable requests of workers or fix mistakes, so it is important to confirm these changes are reflected and your demands are met.
• The company may expand, and the contract may change to make you eligible for promotion or increases, so being aware lets you ensure the employer complies.
• The employer may have indicated a decrease in overtime hours, and familiarising yourself with this means you are not exploited by exceeding the stipulated overtime.
• Being up to date with your contract means that if you want to leave for a better opportunity, you know you can be released without being penalised.
• Reviewing it helps you reaffirm what is expected of you and reassess whether the duties are what you agreed to, protecting you from loopholes you may have missed.
(2 x 3) (6) [20]
subQuestions.topic: Labour laws and the job contract

questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 3: The importance of investigating other views and insights (the human life cycle)
questions.passageText:
THE IMPORTANCE OF INVESTIGATING OTHER VIEWS AND INSIGHTS

The study of the human life cycle offers a wealth of value for our personal understanding of this ever-changing discipline, which mainly includes childhood, adolescence and adulthood.

Being open to other views and insights is the single most important quality we may need as we continue to learn and gain knowledge about the human life cycle throughout our lives. The beauty of investigating other views, insights and traditions related to the human life cycle is that it allows us to find out so many new things and take in so many new perspectives that could assist us through life.

We are living in a world that forces us to question many things that we have come to know throughout our lives, and it should be natural to assume that not everyone shares our upbringing. It may even shock us to realise that the people we may meet in our lifetime may believe in or do things that we may not understand. Since birth we were taught everything we currently know, so seeing things from others' point of view may take time, energy and tolerance.

[Adapted from https://www.thoughtcatalog.com. Accessed on 15 February 2022.]

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term human life cycle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• The stages of growth and change that characterise a human life from beginning to end.
• A person's growth and progression through the different stages of development in life.
• The developmental stages that occur during a person's lifetime.
• The different stages of life that a human being goes through from birth to death.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

subQuestions.questionText: Indicate how an adolescent could deal effectively with an identity crisis as part of the life cycle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any TWO of:
• Get clarity within yourself about what you do and do not like.
• Focus on the things that give meaning to your life.
• Identify support networks and take part in different activities to get to know yourself better (family, friends, community, church, support groups).
• Stay true to yourself and accept who you truly are.
• Speak up about your feelings and views on life.
• Determine what makes you happy.
• Avoid judging or being too hard on yourself.
• Ask for help when you cannot cope with certain things.
• Revisit your values, beliefs, culture or religion for guidance.
• Be mindful of how you deal with peer pressure and influences.
• Do not feel obligated to live up to anybody else's expectations.
(2 x 1) (2)
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why it is important to have knowledge about the human life cycle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. It may help you to:
• Be better prepared for what to expect during each phase, helping you accept the course of life.
• Accept the physical and emotional changes we go through, making it easier to make peace with the inevitability of each stage.
• Gain a better understanding of why you experience life the way you do, so you can find appropriate ways to deal with these experiences.
• Discover important aspects about yourself and others, clarifying why you and others behave the way you do.
• Gain insight into how others, society and your community contribute to your physical and mental development, essential to growing holistically.
• Realise that you should continue to learn and grow throughout life and apply what you have learnt.
• Understand your own life experiences, better preparing you for future difficulties and challenges.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO possible reasons why most people may feel obligated to follow traditional practices.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. People may:
• Be afraid of being disowned, rejected or judged by family, peers or society, so keeping to traditions avoids hostility and unnecessary conflict.
• Feel it is their duty to religiously follow the traditions in their culture, to ensure they are passed on from generation to generation.
• Feel that existing traditional rules offer the guidance they need to live by, making them feel safe and secure in their life decisions.
• Find it easier to cling to systems and structures already in place, so they do not have to figure out new ways of dealing with life's challenges.
• Feel they need to maintain certain practices or superstitions for the greater good and welfare of the family or society, so misfortune does not befall them.
• Do it out of respect for their ancestors or fear of generational curses, wanting to be at peace knowing they are contributing to the generational legacy.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

subQuestions.questionText: Assess the role of the media in promoting tolerance for different traditional practices and/or views.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. The media has the power to:
• Influence society and shape public opinion about what is socially acceptable, persuading people to be unprejudiced about and respect other traditional practices and views.
• Sway people into accepting that the reality of others differs from theirs, helping people see things differently and not violate other people's rights.
• Focus people's attention on the positive aspects of different traditions, minimising traditional biases among people of different belief systems.
• Speak to the unconscious, ignorant attitudes people hold towards other views and traditions, getting them to reflect on their own conduct.
• Deliberately spread ideas about the importance of equality and diversity, creating new narratives and positive attitudes about inclusion.
• Change the associations people make about diverse backgrounds and customs, since the media may be regarded as a reliable source of information.
• Help eliminate social bias relating to different views and traditions, as the media is well placed to influence society to create a new reality about these differences.
• Promote nation building through the coverage of various traditional sports.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

subQuestions.questionText: How could investigating other views and insights regarding life assist with your emotional development? In EACH answer, also indicate how this development could be key to success in all areas of your life.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award THREE marks each for TWO well-explained responses (how it aids emotional development + link to success in all areas of life). It could assist you to:
• Become more aware of how you react to other people, helping you look honestly at how you think and interact with them, so you can build and maintain meaningful relationships.
• Do self-evaluation on how you look at life and step out of your comfort zone, letting you acknowledge your weaknesses and strengths and guiding you to improve and become a better person.
• Identify with and understand the needs of those around you, so you are more open to and accepting of their needs and become more empathetic.
• Practise humility, enabling you to relate better to others and refrain from stereotyping or being judgemental.
• Become a more active listener, so you are more open to others' views and improve your ability to communicate effectively.
• Be more honest about how your actions affect others, helping you become more thoughtful and make ethical, constructive decisions that impact others positively.
• Be mentally strong and mindful of how you react to challenging situations in a diverse context, so you become more tolerant, understanding and accepting of the opinions of others.
• Become more self-motivated and confident, empowering you to be more efficient and stay focused on long-term personal and career goals.
(2 x 3) (6) [20]
subQuestions.topic: The human life cycle and openness to other views

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 4: Staying competitive on e-business platforms (entrepreneurship and e-businesses)
questions.passageText:
SECTION C: Answer any TWO questions in this section. Responses must be in paragraphs; marks are awarded only for responses written in full sentences. If all three questions are answered, only the first TWO are marked.

STAYING COMPETITIVE ON E-BUSINESS PLATFORMS

Entrepreneurship in the cultural and creative industries in South Africa is where individuals have established competitive businesses that are grounded in the arts, creatively inspired and relevant to the cultural heritage of a specific community. In the current global market, this industry has become increasingly competitive for entrepreneurs on e-business platforms.

Glossary: e-business platforms — an online space that allows entrepreneurs to manage their businesses.

[Adapted from https://www.trade.gov.za. Accessed on 22 March 2022.]

Write paragraphs on entrepreneurship and e-businesses using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: State FOUR ways in which a value-based approach could guide an entrepreneur to run a successful e-business.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. It may guide entrepreneurs to:
• Show the same respect for self and others they engage with and treat customers with dignity.
• Practise persistence, perseverance, diligence and fairness in the digital business world.
• Be courageous and bold in pursuing business opportunities online.
• Build trusting, honest relationships with customers, vendors and service providers they trade with online.
• Be self-disciplined and avoid online activities that may jeopardise the business.
• Maintain their credibility and integrity and protect their reputation when doing online transactions.
• Take accountability for the quality of products they market online.
• Communicate politely and display an accommodating attitude with online customers.
• Honour timelines for enquiries, delivery and queries.
• Be reliable and dependable to online customers.
• Be flexible in dealing with online customers.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse how entrepreneurs could use culture to stay competitive on current e-business platforms.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Entrepreneurs could:
• Transform everyday cultural products into modern cultural designs marketed on social media, attracting international customers who would not otherwise buy South African cultural products, broadening or establishing a more viable global client base.
• Create profitable blogs or vlogs sharing recipes about cultural or traditional food on social media, attracting a wide range of paying followers and optimising the possibility of making money online.
• Host live or online cultural or fashion shows, or offer online language courses that people register for at a cost, reaching a wider range of customers and generating more profit at lower marketing costs.
• Document cultural stories or create animations on cultural activities, events and places to sell to tourist centres, which use them on their online platforms, exposing the business to the global market.
• Create e-cards and templates with traditional prints, expressions or slogans for special occasions, which are unique and sought after by a specific client base, guaranteeing a profit from this niche market.
• Print cultural dialects or slang on cultural dress and products and post them on free Blogger sites, gaining passive income from ad-clicks and increasing earning potential on e-platforms.
• Market traditional herbal medicine, handmade items or cultural kitchenware live on TikTok, Instagram or Facebook, earning money through user support (likes, gifts, stars) that is converted to real money, making more sales.
• Host talk shows or stand-up comedy using cultural humour to attract online audiences, an exclusive service that gives a competitive edge in the entertainment industry.
• Use cultural material to design modern clothing patterns and styles advertised on e-platforms, attracting customers worldwide and expanding the client base.
• Use cultural practices (fasting, prayer, ceremonies) to receive blessings on their ventures, which, according to their beliefs, opens up more business opportunities online.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate TWO factors within a cultural group that may have an impact on one's decision to become an entrepreneur.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks (evaluation) a candidate must give a statement and qualify it, then give a second statement and qualify it. Any TWO of:
• An inability to communicate in a preferred language may hamper communication with potential customers and hurt the establishment of a diverse target market; on the other hand, employing staff from different language groups could help one run a successful business in a preferred location.
• Inferiority complexes within certain cultural groups could make some people believe they are destined for poverty and lack inspiration to improve their finances; however, some overcome these feelings and are spurred on to pursue entrepreneurship to change their circumstances.
• A lack of work ethos in certain groups may cause financial dependency and missed entrepreneurial opportunities; whereas others, uncomfortable with their situation and wanting financial independence, are motivated to start their own businesses.
• A lack of family motivation, pressure to follow a certain career, or discouraging women from working could deter one from becoming an entrepreneur so that one gives up easily; whereas others are motivated to prove to the family that they can realise their dream and push against all odds.
• In some families, the financial risk of starting a business is discouraged for fear of failure and worsening the family's financial burden; whereas some are willing to invest in a potential opportunity and gain the chance to prosper as a small business owner.
• Fear of exclusion or being looked down upon if a venture fails creates doubt in those interested in business; whereas others use the experience of those who failed to prove one should not give up at the first attempt and can succeed by improving their skills.
• Religious or cultural views may discourage investment in certain businesses seen as promoting unacceptable practices; whereas some overcome this without compromising their beliefs by meeting community needs purely on a business level.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 5: Collaboration as a conflict resolution skill
questions.passageText:
COLLABORATION: A VITAL INTERPERSONAL SKILL IN THIS ERA

Verbal and non-verbal communication skills are important when having to collaborate. In this new digital era, the ability to collaborate and delegate are even more important in ensuring the success of group projects.

[Adapted from https://pressbooks.com/essential-skills-and-collaboration. Accessed on 22 March 2022.]

Write paragraphs on collaboration as a conflict resolution skill using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: State FOUR reasons why it is important to consider non-verbal communication within a team.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. It could:
• Show you how a person is really perceiving information.
• Give you a better understanding of how a person has interpreted what is communicated.
• Show how a person really feels about a situation.
• Prevent a breakdown in communication.
• Help you be aware of certain cultural gestures and body language.
• Prevent misunderstanding of reactions based on different cultural beliefs or traditions.
• Help you understand that certain behaviour is not necessarily meant to offend you.
• Give you clues about how each team member responds to the way you communicate.
• Give you a truer reflection of what the person may actually be thinking.
• Be a more spontaneous response to what is being said or done.
• Add more meaning to what the person is saying.
• Increase team morale and trustworthiness.
• Eliminate communication gaps and conflict.
• Enhance effective discussion and a peaceful work environment.
• Reinforce team conversations.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse how working from home in this new digital era may affect how you collaborate on a group project.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). You may:
• Be able to work from anywhere in the world and still participate, still meeting the timeframes and completing your tasks within the stipulated time.
• Have limited opportunities to brainstorm with the team, which hurts you if you depend on working closely with others, leading to reduced performance and a negative impact on the project outcome.
• Struggle to maintain normal team interactions, so you do not stay connected, lose motivation to contribute, and participate minimally.
• Spend less time working together with group members since you mostly work alone, making it hard to give valuable input and resulting in ineffective team functioning.
• Be unable to meet as often to discuss important aspects, since it is hard to agree on a suitable online time, leaving you feeling isolated from the group.
• Have limited access to other members' information and expertise that you rely on, affecting your contribution and the overall quality of the project.
• Experience a lack of communication as some members do not adhere to meeting times, making it hard to stay motivated and affecting your progress.
• Have inadequate resources at home, affecting your participation and causing you to miss deadlines, risking completion within the timeframe.
• Be unsure about the roles of other members, developing distrust, doing less than your best and affecting the collective outcome.
• Face technical glitches during online meetings that reduce cooperation and slow your progress.
• Positive analysis is also accepted, e.g.: spend less time and money travelling, giving you more time to complete work; experience fewer distractions, keeping you focused and boosting creativity; access a wider range of information for a more current task; feel more comfortable making inputs if you have social anxiety.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the importance of delegating as a collaborative skill in teamwork.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks (evaluation) a candidate must give a statement and qualify it, then give a second statement and qualify it. Delegating:
• Provides advantages to both the leader and the team by helping manage the workload; however, if not done effectively, work may be given to people not best suited to the task.
• Adds to the professional growth of team members and helps the leader identify top performers; however, if it is not seen as a way to discover strengths and weaknesses, members are deprived of the chance to develop.
• Improves members' competency by letting them gain new skills; on the other hand, if existing abilities are not used efficiently, members feel incapable of contributing.
• Is one of the best strategies to empower members to become leaders and showcase leadership skills; however, if roles are not rotated, other members may not realise they also have leadership qualities.
• Helps determine who the dependable team players are; however, delegating without proper knowledge of members' characteristics means the wrong members may be entrusted with a task.
• Helps members improve their ability to work within a team and value working hand in hand; however, if members misunderstand its significance, they do not learn to work harmoniously.
• Improves the group's general productivity as tasks are shared by capability; however, if members are not allowed to use their expertise optimally, the team does not produce the desired outcomes.
• Helps execute tasks within a given timeframe and meet deadlines; however, if tasks are not distributed fairly, the team collectively fails to meet targets.
• Is an opportunity to give developmental feedback that contributes to individual growth; however, if members do not appreciate its purpose, they miss the chance for growth.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 6: Social media platforms and social media footprint
questions.passageText:
MY PHONE, MY PHOTOS, MY INFORMATION, MY PRIVACY, MY SOCIAL MEDIA FOOTPRINT ...

How big is the problem of young people's social media footprint and personal cellphone use at work really? More especially during working hours. Although workers have a right to privacy with regard to using their personal electronic devices at work, they can, however, not claim unlimited freedom to engage in personal interactions on social media platforms during working hours.

[Adapted from https://www.labourguide.co.za. Accessed on 1 March 2022.]

Write paragraphs on social media platforms and social media footprint using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: State FOUR ways in which young people could manage their social media footprint more effectively.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. You could:
• Control and limit public access to your personal information on social media.
• Refrain from posting scandalous information or getting involved in scandalous discussions.
• Conduct yourself respectfully towards others and accept only friends/acquaintances who conduct themselves respectably.
• Share charitable deeds, activities and projects you or others are involved with.
• Celebrate your own and others' successes and achievements on your profile.
• Share information about online courses you or others could consider for upskilling.
• Take part in online events, surveys or petitions that aim to address social challenges.
• Refrain from engaging in controversial, disrespectful or harmful conversations.
• Avoid posting, sharing or responding to hurtful or inappropriate material.
• Refrain from encouraging others who demonstrate unacceptable conduct on these platforms.
• Limit the number of social media applications you use.
(4 x 1) (4)
subQuestions.topic: Social media footprint and the workplace

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse TWO possible negative implications that spending time on social media during working hours may have for a workplace.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). It could cause:
• Workers to be less productive, since attending to many messages and calls is distracting and workers are not fully occupied with scheduled work, resulting in many working hours being lost daily.
• Workers to not pay full attention to their work, preventing them from prioritising duties, leading to missed deadlines and hampering the overall functionality of the company.
• Workers to make unnecessary mistakes as they work with divided attention, leading to a poor standard of work and possible financial losses for the company.
• Hostility between workers, as others are expected to help get the job done to prevent a ripple effect, leading to unnecessary stressful situations in the workplace.
• An impression that the company or all its workers have a poor, unethical work culture, ruining the company's reputation so clients do not want to do business with it, leading to business losses, lost networking opportunities or losing out on excellent prospective workers.
• Interference with a worker's interaction with customers, as they feel the urge to always respond to social media, compromising their professional conduct and leaving clients dissatisfied with the service.
(2 x 4) (8)
subQuestions.topic: Social media footprint and the workplace

subQuestions.questionText: Critically discuss why it is important for an employer to enforce limitations on the use of personal electronic devices in order to protect a company.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses (statement + elaborate + qualify + outcome). Any TWO of:
• To restrict irresponsible use of a company's sensitive information, personal devices should be closely monitored, as disloyal workers could retain confidential information on their devices, undermining company policy.
• Workers could claim a right to privacy over work done on their personal devices for the company and use that information to market as their own, undermining trust and violating the company's intellectual property rights.
• Workers may assume they can store work-related information on their own devices and could unknowingly share it with competitors, giving unauthorised access to the company's intellectual property, to the company's detriment.
• It may prevent workers with ulterior motives from underhandedly using confidential information against the company, which could be deceitful practice and grounds for lawful dismissal.
• Where personal devices present a safety hazard in the workplace, stricter regulations are needed, as the employer is legally accountable for the occupational safety of all workers.
• Workers could cause irrevocable damage by sharing condemning information about the company, so the employer has the right to confiscate a device to ensure the information is removed and protect everyone's privacy.
• Workers may feel entitled to the privacy of data on their own devices obtained without permission, so the employer includes the limitation in a policy document, making it mandatory for all workers to comply.
• Workers could compromise company security by sharing information about the company's infrastructure, giving others knowledge of security aspects and jeopardising the safety of the premises.
• Workers could take pictures, videos or voice notes of sensitive activities and share them freely without considering the consequences, so the company must confiscate such material to maintain confidentiality about its operations.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]
